description:
Your bed: bed bugs can travel over 100 feet in a night but tend to live within 8 feet of where people sleep. This is a born-as guide to the common bed bug in a house: how far they walk, where they hide, how they hitch a ride, the delayed bite, heat that stays official, the eggs, what not to do, and what actually helps. Meatball lives all eight from the couch, with his dog, Noodle, as the stand-in and his cat, Sauce, as everybody else.

Checked facts in this video:
- Lead is the common bed bug (Cimex lectularius). EPA's appearance page is titled "Appearance of Bed Bugs (Cimex lectularius L.)." University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636 uses "the common bed bug (Cimex lectularius)." CDC About Bed Bugs says "Bed bugs (Cimex species)" and does not name lectularius or hemipterus on the extracted page. Distance, bite-delay, and other CDC lines stay tagged CDC and may be said of bed bugs generally with that tag. This video does not mix in the tropical bed bug (C. hemipterus).
- CDC: "Bed bugs can travel over 100 feet in a night but tend to live within 8 feet of where people sleep." Keep "can," "over 100 feet," "in a night," "tend to live," "within 8 feet," and "of where people sleep." The spoken hook is a tight 11-word line that keeps both distance halves, "can," "over," "a night," "within 8," and "your bed." The official "in a night," "tend to live," and "of where people sleep" wording is on the hook card from 0:00 and is spoken in full right after the eight-things line, and again in chapter 1, with both halves on the same sentence.
- That 8-foot half is not the same as they never go farther. A different official page (University of Kentucky) says they prefer to hide close to where they feed, but if necessary will crawl longer distances in search of a meal. During the day, they tend to hide close to where people sleep. That page does not give a 100-foot or 8-foot figure, and this video does not invent one for it. Initially they tend to be concentrated around beds, sofas, and other sleeping and resting areas, but if infestations are allowed to persist, they may disperse elsewhere, making elimination more difficult.
- Adult bed bugs are about 3/16-inch long and reddish-brown, with oval, flattened bodies. Their coloration is similar to an apple seed although their size is closer to a lentil (University of Kentucky). Keep "about." A different official page (EPA) says adult bed bugs, in general, are about the size of an apple seed (5-7 mm or 3/16-1/4 inch long); flat and brown if not fed recently; balloon-like, reddish-brown, and more elongated if fed recently. Those two size lines are not averaged. CDC's 1 mm to 7 mm range, roughly the size of Lincoln's head on a penny, covers nymphs through adults and is not stacked in speech with apple seed and lentil as one official simile (D1). It is kept here.
- Their flattened bodies enable them to fit into tiny crevices no wider than a toothpick. Bed bugs don't have nests like ants or bees, but do tend to congregate in habitual hiding places like mattresses, box springs, bed frames and headboards (University of Kentucky). A different official page (CDC) says they hide during the day in places on or around the bed, and can hide in the seams of mattresses, box springs, bed frames and headboards, dresser tables, inside cracks or crevices, and behind wallpaper. Their slim flat bodies allow them to fit into very small spaces.
- Adult females lay eggs in secluded places, depositing one, two or more per day, potentially hundreds during their lifetime. The eggs are tiny (about the size of a dust spec), whitish and hard to see without magnification, especially on light-colored materials. At room temperature, eggs hatch in about a week. Newly emerged nymphs are straw-colored and no bigger than a pinhead (University of Kentucky). The page typo "dust spec" is kept as the page's wording, not silently corrected. A different official page (EPA) says bed bug eggs, in general, are tiny, the size of a pinhead, pearl-white, and marked by an eye spot if more than five days old; young bed bugs (nymphs), in general, are smaller, translucent or whitish-yellow, and if not recently fed, can be nearly invisible to the naked eye. Bed bugs don't fly, or jump like fleas, but can crawl rapidly over floors, walls, ceilings and other surfaces.
- The bugs are efficient hitchhikers and are easily transported into dwellings on luggage, clothing, beds, furniture, and belongings. Acquiring secondhand beds and furniture is another way they can be transported. They can also be inadvertently carried in on clothing, shoes, a wheelchair, backpacks, luggage, and other belongings (University of Kentucky). A different official page (CDC) says they spread by getting into the seams and folds of luggage, overnight bags, folded clothes, bedding, furniture, and anywhere else they can hide. Most people do not realize they are transporting bed bugs. That page also says "infecting areas as they travel"; "infecting" there means spreading the infestation, not spreading a disease, and that wording is not spoken in this video.
- Unlike cockroaches and flies that feed on filth, there is often no relationship between bed bugs and cleanliness. Since the bugs feed solely on blood, pristine dwellings can be as vulnerable to infestation as are places of squalor (University of Kentucky). A different official page (CDC) says how clean a place is does not determine whether bed bugs are present, and that they are in five-star hotels and resorts. That is not "every hotel has them." You can find bed bugs anywhere, from North and South America to Africa, Asia, and Europe (CDC). Everyone is at risk for getting bed bugs when visiting an infested area. You are at higher risk if you travel frequently and share living and sleeping space where other people have previously slept.
- Bed bugs are active mainly at night. During the day, they tend to hide close to where people sleep. They usually bite people at night while they are sleeping. Hungry bed bugs may also feed during the day, especially if this is when the occupant normally sleeps (University of Kentucky). This video does not invent a 4 a.m. feeding clock. A different official page (CDC) says bed bugs bite people and animals at night while they sleep, feeding on their blood.
- One of the easiest ways to identify a bed bug infestation is by bite marks on the face, neck, arms, hands, or any other body parts after sleeping. However, these bite marks may take as long as 14 days to develop in some people (CDC). Keep "may," "as long as 14 days," and "in some people." Look for other clues too: exoskeletons, bugs in folds, rusty-colored blood spots, and a sweet musty odor. This is not "if you have no marks, you don't have bed bugs."
- They feed by piercing the skin with an elongated beak. Engorgement takes about three to 10 minutes, but because the bite is painless, people seldom realize they are being bitten. Bed bugs normally do not reside on or attach to people like lice or ticks; immediately after feeding they crawl to a secluded location to digest their meal (University of Kentucky).
- Bites can cause itching, loss of sleep, and, rarely, allergic reactions. Bed bugs are not known to spread diseases to people. Allergic symptoms can include enlarged bite marks, painful swellings at the bite site, and, on rare occasions, anaphylaxis. If you think you are having an allergic reaction to bed bug bites, speak with your healthcare provider (CDC). Keep "can," "rarely," and "not known to spread diseases." This video does not copy the live-page typo "loss off sleep."
- EPA IPM: put bedding and clothing in the dryer at high temperatures for 30 minutes to kill bed bugs (just washing will generally not kill bed bugs). Heat infested articles (furniture, luggage, items that can't go in a dryer) and/or areas (a room, or a whole house) to at least 120 F (about 49 C) for 90 minutes to ensure that eggs are killed. The higher the temperature, the shorter the time needed. This is often done using a heat-generating device or a specially constructed heating unit. Those two heat recipes stay separate and are not averaged. Whole-house heat on this page is that device method, not a home thermostat.
- EPA DIY: you can use a clothes dryer on high heat. Do-it-yourself heat treatments might not work. Professionals have access to more intensive and proven methods that can even treat whole houses with heat. Do not try to kill bed bugs by increasing your indoor temperature with a thermostat, propane space heater, or fireplace — this does not work and is dangerous. The car-and-bags method on that page is hedged "might not work" / "depends on your climate" and is not recommended in this video as a sure trick. Professionals can treat an entire residence, but it must be done properly. Heat treatments have no residual effects, so practices must be in place to avoid re-introducing bed bugs.
- EPA DIY steam: steam temperature must be at least 130 F but should not have a forceful airflow, or it may scatter bed bugs. Use a diffuser. That 130 F is steam on bed bugs, not a laundry wash, and it is not spoken in this video; it is kept here and is not mixed with any other pest's numbers.
- Cold treatments: EPA IPM says below 0 F (about -19 C) for at least 4 days can eliminate some infestations. Home freezers may not be cold enough to reliably kill bed bugs. Always use a thermometer. A different official page (EPA DIY) says you must leave the items in a sealed bag in the freezer at 0 F for three days, and that many home refrigerator freezers are not cold enough; always use a thermometer. Those 4-day and 3-day figures are not blended (D2). The three-day line is not spoken in this video; it is kept here. This video does not copy the IPM typo "may not cold be enough."
- In temperature-controlled buildings, a more typical duration without feeding is about 1 to 4 months, and it is usually impractical to leave homes unoccupied in hopes of starving an infestation. When vacant apartments are empty, bed bugs often disperse to nearby units, or reduce their activity until the unit is reoccupied (University of Kentucky). A different official page (CDC) says they can live several months without a blood meal. Those are related, not identical, and are not treated as one number (D3). Sleeping with the lights on is not likely to deter hungry bed bugs; they will adjust their feeding cycle to the host's sleep patterns.
- When selecting and using pesticides, read and strictly follow the label directions. The label tells you if the pesticide is approved for use against bed bugs (don't use it if it is not). Never use a pesticide indoors that is intended for outdoor use. It is very dangerous and won't solve your bed bug problem (EPA). If needed, hire a pest management professional or use pesticides carefully according to the label. Look for EPA-registered pesticides that have bed bugs listed on the label. Use foggers (bug bombs) only with extreme care and only if bed bugs are listed on the label. Improper use can harm your health or cause a fire or explosion. Foggers should not be your only method; the spray will not reach the cracks and crevices where bed bugs hide.
- Prevent bed bugs by regularly looking for signs of infestation. Removal from dwellings can be expensive and inconvenient (CDC).
